sunforge-story.text: Community-first weird western storytelling. Each page should preserve the immediate human stakes before serving the larger mystery. Dialogue must sound like spoken English rather than stylized telegram prose: do not manufacture terseness by deleting pronouns, articles, auxiliary verbs or ordinary grammar. Brandon is economical because he does not volunteer much, not because he cannot form complete sentences; let him be polite, mundane, dry, occasionally longer when he has something to say, and occasionally annoyed when a stray remark invites a personal question. Early Eva/Jessie dialogue may fail the Bechdel test hard by design: they talk about Brandon, construct theories and counter-theories, compare what he says with what he does, and through that process reveal themselves to each other. Eva tends toward possibility and adventure; Jessie tends toward observed behavior and human explanations, though her continued presence exposes how curious she really is. Their conversation should gradually become a friendship before either names it. As Brandon becomes legible to them as an actual person, the identity question should lose its monopoly on their dialogue and all three characters should become freer to have independent wants, histories and relationships. Raina's control is human investigative pressure, not scientific omniscience. Samuel's manipulation depends on genuine listening and care. Avoid placeholder call-and-response, aphorism factories and dialogue in which every line merely advances the mystery. Give each speaker distinct sentence shape, priorities, humor, avoidance and emotional temperature. Sunforges remain observed background facts unless the page itself earns more. Keep thematic-development language in direction and series documentation rather than putting it verbatim in a character's mouth; characters should reach ideas through the particulars of the conversation, not recite the architecture of the book. Caption narration may appear as dialogueInline speaker CAPTION. The narrator is a dry western storyteller: authoritative about ordinary facts, names, visible history, elapsed time and immediate context, but not about the larger mystery. Use captions to introduce people, compress time, contrast rumor with observed fact, or create mild irony. The narrator must not reveal mystery answers, explain themes, invent pseudo-scientific causality, or tell the reader what to feel. Not every page needs captions; each caption must do work the panels or balloons do not.
